question: The following excerpt and accompanying illustration are derived from Emilie Reas’ work, "How the brain learns to read: development of the 'word form area'", published in PLOS Neuro Community in 2018. The capability to recognize, process, and interpret written language is a distinctive human ability that is acquired effortlessly during early childhood. However, anyone who has embarked on the journey of learning a new language knows that the human brain is not inherently “hardwired” to comprehend written text. The intricate processes behind how the brain develops this specialized skill remain somewhat enigmatic. While researchers have pinpointed specific brain regions responsible for processing written words, the mechanisms through which selectivity for language emerges are not yet fully understood. Previous research has indicated that the ventral visual cortex is crucial for the recognition of various visual stimuli, including objects, faces, and locations. Within this cortex, a particular subregion located in the left hemisphere, referred to as the "visual word form area" (VWFA), demonstrates a distinct selectivity for written words. However, this area exhibits significant plasticity. It has been suggested that different stimuli compete for representation in this adaptable region, leading to a "winner takes all" scenario based on the most potent input. Thus, the way in which a location within the brain is ultimately mapped depends heavily on its usage in early childhood. Despite this hypothesis, it remains unconfirmed, and the development of specialized brain regions for reading in children continues to be poorly understood. In their investigation, Dehaene-Lambertz and colleagues observed the reading abilities and brain changes in ten six-year-old children to track the emergence of word specialization during a vital developmental stage. Throughout their first year of schooling, the children underwent evaluation every two months through reading assessments and functional MRI scans while viewing both words and non-word images (such as houses, objects, faces, and bodies). As anticipated, reading skills improved during the initial year of first grade, as evidenced by rising reading speed, increased word span, and enhanced phoneme knowledge, among other measures. [Sentence 1] Remarkably, even at such an early age, when reading skills were just beginning to form, written words triggered extensive activation in the left side of the brain. This activation intensified throughout the school year, with the most substantial increase occurring shortly after the school commenced. Critically, there were no comparable increases in activation in response to other types of stimuli, demonstrating that these changes were specifically tied to reading ability rather than a general developmental or educational effect. Right from the start of formal schooling, the brain volume associated with reading also experienced a notable increase. Moreover, there was a correlation between reading speed and heightened activity, especially within the VWFA. The researchers established that the patterns of activation in response to written words became more consistent with learning. [Sentence 2] Conversely, the activation patterns corresponding to other categories remained relatively stable, except for numbers, which might indicate a general specialization for symbols (both words and numbers), or a correlation with the concurrent enhancement of mathematical skills. What factors determine why one brain region is predisposed to assume a specialized role in reading words over another? Prior to attending school, there was no significant preference for any category within regions that would eventually become responsive to words. [Sentence 3] However, brain areas which were destined to remain non-word regions exhibited more stable reactions to non-word stimuli even before the children learned to read. Therefore, it is possible that the brain utilizes vacant cortical space to facilitate the newly acquired skill of reading. These discoveries contribute a vital piece to understanding how reading abilities are developed in the child’s evolving brain. While it has been established that reading activates a specialized area for words, this research illustrates that such activation occurs without altering the organization of areas that were already specialized for different functions. The authors propose a sophisticated model to explain the developmental brain changes that occur during the acquisition of reading skills. In an illiterate child, there exist adjacent columns or zones within the cortex that may be attuned to specific categories or remain unassigned in function. With the onset of literacy, these previously unutilized subregions become attuned to words, while the regions that had already been specialized maintain their stability. [Sentence 4] The swift emergence of the word area following just a brief learning phase emphasizes the exceptional plasticity of the developing cortex. For individuals who gain literacy in adulthood, the same VWFA exists. Nevertheless, unlike children, the relationship between reading speed and activation in this area is weaker in adults, and a single adult case study highlighted a significantly slower and more gradual progression of the VWFA over a lengthened learning duration of several months. Regardless of the reasons, this region appears ready to quickly adopt new representations of symbolic words, and this readiness may peak during a specific developmental window in childhood. This finding underscores the critical importance of a robust education during youth. The authors hypothesize that “the effectiveness of education could also hinge on the optimal timing to leverage peak neural plasticity. question: This passage is adapted from Adam K. Fetterman and Kai Sassenberg, “The Reputational Consequences of Failed Replications and Wrongness Admission among Scientists", first published in December 2015 by PLOS ONE. We like to think of science as a purely rational. However, scientists are human and often identify with their work. Therefore, it should not be controversial to suggest that emotions are involved in replication discussions. Adding to this inherently emotionally volatile situation, the recent increase in the use of social media and blogs by scientists has allowed for instantaneous, unfiltered, and at times emotion-based commentary on research. Certainly social media has the potential to lead to many positive outcomes in science-among others, to create a more open science. To some, however, it seems as if this ease of communication is also leading to the public tar and feathering of scientists. Whether these assertions are true is up for debate, but we assume they are a part of many scientists’ subjective reality. Indeed, when failed replications are discussed in the same paragraphs as questionable research practices, or even fraud, it is hard to separate the science from the scientist. Questionable research practices and fraud are not about the science; they are about the scientist. We believe that these considerations are at least part of the reason that we find the overestimation effect that we do, here. Even so, the current data suggests that while many are worried about how a failed replication would affect their reputation, it is probably not as bad as they think. Of course, the current data cannot provide evidence that there are no negative effects; just that the negative impact is overestimated. That said, everyone wants to be seen as competent and honest, but failed replications are a part of science. In fact, they are how science moves forward! While we imply that these effects may be exacerbated by social media, the data cannot directly speak to this. However, any one of a number of cognitive biases may add support to this assumption and explain our findings. For example, it may be that a type of availability bias or pluralistic ignorance of which the more vocal and critical voices are leading individuals to judge current opinions as more negative than reality. As a result, it is easy to conflate discussions about direct replications with “witch- hunts” and overestimate the impact on one’s own reputation. Whatever the source may be, it is worth looking at the potential negative impact of social media in scientific conversations. If the desire is to move science forward, scientists need to be able to acknowledge when they are wrong. Theories come and go, and scientists learn from their mistakes (if they can even be called “mistakes”). This is the point of science. However, holding on to faulty ideas flies in the face of the scientific method. Even so, it often seems as if scientists have a hard time admitting wrongness. This seems doubly true when someone else fails to replicate a scientist’s findings. Even so, it often seems as if scientists have a hard time admitting wrongness. This seems doubly true when someone else fails to replicate a scientist’s findings. In some cases, this may be the proper response. Just as often, though, it is not. In most cases, admitting wrongness will have relatively fewer ill effects on one’s reputation than not admitting and it may be better for reputation. It could also be that wrongness admission repairs damage to reputation. It may seem strange that others consider it less likely that questionable research practices, for example, were used when a scientist admits that they were wrong. However, it does make sense from the standpoint that wrongness admission seems to indicate honesty. Therefore, if one is honest in one domain, they are likely honest in other domains. Moreover, the refusal to admit might indicate to others that the original scientist is trying to cover something up. The lack of significance of most of the interactions in our study suggests that it even seems as if scientists might already realize this. Therefore, we can generally suggest that scientists admit they are wrong, but only when the evidence suggests they should. The chart below maps how scientists view others' work (left) and how they suspect others will view their own work (right) if the researcher (the scientist or another, depending on the focus) admitted to engaging in questionable research practices.
